passages.t: The Lord's anger brings the city down
passages.happening:
The second poem opens with the same cry as the first: “How the Lord has covered the Daughter of Zion with the cloud of His anger!” (verse 1). He has thrown down the glory of Israel, and ‘He has abandoned His footstool in the day of His anger’ (verse 1).

The poem piles up what God has done. ‘Without pity the Lord has swallowed up all the dwellings of Jacob’ (verse 2). He has cut off Israel's strength and burned like a fire (verse 3). ‘He has bent His bow like an enemy’ (verse 4). ‘The Lord is like an enemy; He has swallowed up Israel’ (verse 5). He has laid his own tabernacle waste like a garden shelter and made Zion forget her feasts and Sabbaths (verse 6).

‘The Lord has rejected His altar; He has abandoned His sanctuary’ (verse 7). Enemy soldiers shout in the temple courts ‘as on the day of an appointed feast’ (verse 7). God measured the wall for destruction and did not hold back (verse 8). The gates have sunk into the ground. The king and princes are in exile, the law is no more, ‘and even her prophets find no vision from the LORD’ (verse 9).

And the city's leaders mourn. ‘The elders of the Daughter of Zion sit on the ground in silence’ (verse 10), with dust on their heads and sackcloth on their bodies, and the young women bow their heads to the ground.
passages.hearers:
Chapter 1 dwelt on the city's loneliness and shame. Chapter 2 asks who did this. The answer is not only Babylon. In verse after verse the subject of the sentence is the Lord. The first hearers knew why. The covenant had warned of this, and the prophets had announced it. The poem is saying that the fall was not an accident of politics.

The temple was understood as the place where God's presence rested on earth. Calling it his footstool pictures God enthroned in heaven with his feet resting in Jerusalem, and the same word is used of the ark and the temple elsewhere. So to say God abandoned his footstool is to say he walked away from his own house.

The shout in the courts in verse 7 is the noise of soldiers where festival crowds used to sing. The feasts and Sabbaths had been the rhythm of Israel's life with God, and now the calendar of worship itself had stopped. Verse 9 lists what was gone: the king, Zedekiah, blinded and taken to Babylon; the law no more; the prophets with no word.

Sitting on the ground in silence, with dust on the head and sackcloth on the body, were the standard rites of mourning. Sackcloth was a coarse cloth of goat hair. The elders of the city, the men who sat in the gate and judged, now sit in the dirt.
passages.later: A psalm of the same ruin begins, ‘Why have You rejected us forever, O God? Why does Your anger smolder against the sheep of Your pasture?’ (Psalm 74:1). And the prophet Amos had warned of the loss verse 9 grieves: ‘not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the words of the LORD’ (Amos 8:11).
passages.hard:
How can the Bible say that God acted like an enemy and destroyed without pity?

This passage should be read slowly. First, the poet is describing how the disaster felt from inside it, and the Bible lets that experience stand in its own words. He says the Lord is like an enemy. It is a simile, a way of saying what it felt like, not a claim that God's nature had changed. Second, the poem traces the fall to the judgment God had warned of for generations, not to a sudden whim (verse 17). Third, the book sets this beside its own confession that the Lord ‘does not willingly afflict or grieve the sons of men’ (3:33) and that his mercies never fail (3:22).

Interpreters weigh these differently. Some stress God's sovereignty over the disaster. Others stress that God let the consequences of the nation's choices, and Babylon's cruelty, run their course. Both agree that the poem does not make the suffering small.

This is Judah's own Scripture, judging Judah's own sin and grieving Judah's own losses. It was written for people who had lost everything, to help them understand their history and turn back to God. It is not a key for reading anyone else's suffering. It gives no one a warrant to say that any people's suffering, then or now, is a punishment they deserved. And it is never a reason to blame the Jewish people, then or now.
passages.asks: The poet refuses to blame only Babylon. Ask what is gained, and what is risked, when a person sees God's hand in a disaster. And ask whether you would rather speak to God honestly about what you think he has done, or stay silent.

passages.t: The poet's tears over the children, and the false prophets
passages.happening:
Now the poet speaks in his own voice, and he breaks down. ‘My eyes fail from weeping; I am churning within’ (verse 11). His heart is poured out in grief, ‘because children and infants faint in the streets of the city’ (verse 11). Little ones cry to their mothers for bread and wine and faint like the wounded, ‘as their lives fade away in the arms of their mothers’ (verse 12).

He searches for something to compare the city to, anything that might console her, and finds nothing. ‘For your wound is as deep as the sea. Who can ever heal you?’ (verse 13).

Then he names the prophets. ‘The visions of your prophets were empty and deceptive; they did not expose your guilt to ward off your captivity’ (verse 14).

‘All who pass by clap their hands at you in scorn’ (verse 15). They hiss and shake their heads and mock the city once called the perfection of beauty. Her enemies open their mouths and boast that they have swallowed her up (verse 16). And the poet says who stands behind it all: ‘The LORD has done what He planned; He has accomplished His decree, which He ordained in days of old’ (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Siege warfare was the most feared kind of war in the ancient world, because hunger inside the walls killed more people than the fighting, and the weak suffered first. The first hearers had watched it happen to their own children. The poet does not soften it, and he does not explain it. He weeps.

The prophets of verse 14 were men the first hearers had listened to. Jeremiah reports that in the years before the fall, prophets such as Hananiah promised that Babylon's power would soon be broken and the exiles would be home within two years. Others kept saying peace when there was no peace. Their comforting visions kept the people from facing their guilt and turning back while there was still time.

Clapping, hissing and shaking the head were gestures of scorn. The mockers quote the city's old praise of herself. Psalms had called Zion beautiful, the joy of all the earth, and now strangers say it with a sneer.

Verse 17 is the poem's hinge. Days of old points back to the covenant warnings given long before, such as Deuteronomy 28. What has happened is what God said would happen.
passages.later: Jeremiah had warned against the prophets this verse condemns: ‘They dress the wound of My people with very little care’ (Jeremiah 6:14). And Jeremiah wept as this poet weeps: ‘I would weep day and night over the slain daughter of my people’ (Jeremiah 9:1). The psalm the mockers twist had sung, ‘Beautiful in loftiness, the joy of all the earth’ (Psalm 48:2).
passages.hard:
Children and infants faint from hunger in the streets. How can a book of Scripture hold that?

Scripture does not hide that judgment on a society falls on the innocent within it. The children of the siege had not chosen their leaders' policies or their parents' gods. The poet's tears are the point. He does not say the children deserved it, and he does not call it a lesson. He grieves it as a horror, and he brings it to God, as the next verses do.

No reader should take from this chapter that a child's suffering, or a child's death, is a punishment on the child or on the parents. The poem gives no such warrant, and the rest of the Bible gives none.

If you carry grief or guilt about a pregnancy, or about the loss of a child before or after birth, please know that you are met with gentleness here, not judgment. God knows your story too. Please talk with a trusted pastor or friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The false prophets gave a comforting word that hid the truth. Ask where you prefer a comforting word to a true one. And ask whether there is anyone you are failing to warn because you would rather be liked.

passages.t: Pour out your heart, and the city's prayer
passages.happening:
The poet tells the city to cry out. ‘The hearts of the people cry out to the Lord’ (verse 18). He tells the wall of the city to ‘let your tears run down like a river day and night’ (verse 18), and to give itself no rest.

‘Arise, cry out in the night from the first watch of the night. Pour out your heart like water in the presence of the Lord’ (verse 19). ‘Lift up your hands to Him for the lives of your children who are fainting from hunger on the corner of every street’ (verse 19).

So the city prays. ‘Look, O LORD, and consider: Whom have You ever treated like this?’ (verse 20). She names the worst thing the famine did, which Deuteronomy 28:53 had warned of: mothers driven by hunger to eat their own children. These notes name it and do not describe it. She asks whether priests and prophets should be killed in the Lord's sanctuary.

‘Both young and old lie together in the dust of the streets’ (verse 21). Her young men and young women have fallen by the sword. She says God has slain them without compassion. He summoned her attackers from every side, as if calling people to a feast (verse 22). ‘In the day of the LORD’s anger no one escaped or survived’ (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
The night was divided into watches, and the first watch was its beginning. The poet is telling the city to pray all night long, without stopping. To lift up the hands was the posture of prayer and of pleading.

The priests and prophets killed in the sanctuary points to the slaughter when the city fell, which 2 Chronicles 36:17 records. The day of the LORD's anger frames the whole poem: it is named in its first verse and its last.

The city's prayer is almost an accusation. She does not dress it up. She asks God to look at what has happened and to say whether anyone has ever been treated like this. The first hearers had perhaps never heard a prayer like it. It shows that honest protest is itself a way of praying. The poet has just told her to pour out her heart, and this is what pours out.

The curse of Deuteronomy 28 had named this horror as one of the things that would come in a siege if the covenant were broken, and 2 Kings 6 records it in the siege of Samaria. Naming it here is not a celebration of a warning fulfilled. It is the city's cry of anguish laid before God.
passages.later: A psalm teaches the same prayer: ‘Trust in Him at all times, O people; pour out your hearts before Him’ (Psalm 62:8). And in Isaiah the LORD speaks to the city that has drunk ‘from the hand of the LORD the cup of His fury’ (Isaiah 51:17), and tells her to rise.
passages.hard:
The city asks God, Whom have You ever treated like this? Is it right to speak to God that way?

The Bible includes this prayer, and the poet himself has just urged the city to pray it. Lament is not unbelief. The psalms of lament, and Job, speak to God in the same raw way. The prayer is spoken to God, not away from him. That is the difference between a protest of faith and a turning away.

The things the city names are a horror, not a lesson, and the poem does not ask the reader to see them as anything else. Readers carrying their own grief, especially the loss of a child, will find here permission to protest before God.

Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The poet tells the city to pour out her heart like water before the Lord. Ask what keeps you from praying that honestly. And ask whether there is a question you have never dared to ask God out loud.
